extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientific community, research-integrity monitors, postdocs and whistleblowers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for judging the credibility, ethics, and reliability of published biomedical research and the conduct of research groups. Covers evidence standards (raw data, image integrity), responsibilities (PI oversight, authorship), and systemic/institutional factors affecting investigation and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of raw data
rubrics_metrics.description: "If they have raw data to show, there will be no issues." The presence of original/raw experimental data is presented as a key means to resolve concerns about figures or alleged manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals, institutions, and investigators should request and examine raw data to adjudicate allegations; absence of raw data leaves questions unresolved and fuels suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of control data / unique controls per experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-use of control bands or identical control values across multiple publications is flagged as suspicious and potentially misconduct (e.g., questions about "re-use of control bands").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each experiment should have appropriate, documented controls; lab books or logs showing performed controls may be relevant but do not automatically exonerate authors if controls were not included properly in the published record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure and image integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Image manipulation, duplicated bands, or reused figures across papers constitute serious irregularities and possible scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeated control values, identical image elements across different papers, and other signs of duplication. Forensic image analysis may be needed in non-obvious cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency and reproducibility across publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicting conclusions from the same lab/group (e.g., two papers from same year with opposing abstracts) undermine credibility and raise red flags about reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether results are internally consistent and whether independent labs have replicated the findings; inconsistency within a group suggests sloppy methods, selective reporting, or worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal Investigator (PI) responsibility for quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: PIs/managers are ultimately responsible for the quality and integrity of work produced by their labs. Being 'hands-off' (fund-raiser only) is not an excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the PI provided adequate oversight; institutions should hold PIs accountable when a lab shows systemic problems (possible grounds for removal/discipline if oversight is inadequate or negligence is shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics: prioritize quality and reproducibility over publication counts and impact factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting papers or impact factors is criticized as incentivizing quantity over trustworthy science; assessment should emphasize robustness and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and career-evaluation processes should value reproducible, high-quality work rather than raw numbers of publications or journal prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication volume plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremely high publication rates (e.g., dozens of papers per year) are potentially implausible and warrant scrutiny for review articles/coauthorship patterns or possible misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate authorship roles, the mix of reviews vs. original research, and the feasibility of supervising that volume; not proof of misconduct but a trigger for closer inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate authorship attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering authorship to obtain support or including many nominal co-authors is unethical and distorts responsibility for the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate author lists for appropriateness; investigate patterns suggesting honorary authorship or quid-pro-quo authorship arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential conflicts arising from editorial positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership on editorial boards may bias journals' responses and create barriers to independent scrutiny and retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for possible reluctance from journals to act when implicated authors hold editorial positions; independent or external review may be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of institutions and journals in investigating misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals often rely on institutional investigations before retracting papers; different countries/institutions have different processes (and some lack effective research-integrity offices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realize that retraction or correction often requires an institution-led inquiry; where institutional oversight is weak or conflicted, allegations may languish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of whistleblowers
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous or named whistleblowers often initiate investigations and surface irregularities that would otherwise remain hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect and take seriously whistleblower reports; create safe channels for reporting, since whistleblowers are essential but vulnerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power dynamics and vulnerability of trainees
rubrics_metrics.description: Postdocs and trainees (especially immigrants on visas) may feel coerced to produce desired results and fear retaliation, which suppresses reporting of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for systemic vulnerabilities when evaluating allegations; institutions should provide protections so trainees can report misconduct without jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical control measurements across papers indicate possible data recycling
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance of the same numerical control values or control results in multiple publications is highlighted as evidence suggesting reused data rather than independent experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize repeated numerical/control patterns; statistical improbability of identical values across independent experiments can indicate fabrication or recycling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for forensic analysis to detect subtle misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Some irregularities are obvious, but others require forensic examination of images and data to detect manipulation; journals may not act without such analysis or institutional confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When allegations are complex, apply image forensics, raw-data audits, and expert review; absence of forensic work can keep problematic publications uncorrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation practices and self-citation inflation
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive self-citation (e.g., >10%) can inflate perceived impact and visibility, which may distort assessments of scientific influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine citation patterns when evaluating a researcher's influence; correct for excessive self-citation as part of impact assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial promotion of research for personal gain
rubrics_metrics.description: Using publications as marketing tools (sending papers to companies or MLM networks) is unethical and may indicate intent to commercialize or promote findings irrespective of rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate outreach/marketing behavior connected to publications as potential conflicts of interest or red flags for misuse of research claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological similarity across studies is not proof of misconduct by itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same experimental approach on different compounds or systems is common and not inherently fraudulent, but it doesn't exempt results from scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish acceptable methodological repetition from evidence of data recycling; similarity should prompt evaluation of experimental independence and reporting transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical barriers to retraction (legal and procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may avoid unilateral retraction due to legal risk; they commonly wait for institutional findings before taking corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect delays and the need for institutional leadership; this procedural reality affects how and when literature is corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential conflicts within institutional oversight bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: If institutional research-integrity officials or leaders are themselves implicated or have conflicts, investigations may be compromised and ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and mitigate conflicts of interest in investigative bodies; consider independent external review where internal oversight is compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic reform: develop new strategies for selecting and assessing good scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: The current hiring/promotion system (focused on counts and journals) is implicated in producing incentives for questionable practices; a call to develop new assessment strategies is presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluation systems that reward reproducibility, data-sharing, and methodological rigor rather than sheer productivity metrics.
